Mr. Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate with Mr. Probir Neogi, Advocate, Defendant-Appellant-Petitioner. 
Dr. M. Zahir, Senior Advocate with Mr. Junayed Ahmed Chowdhury, Advocate, Plaintiffs-Respondent-Opposite Parties.
parties:
Zahid Hossain
Vs.
Syed Fazlul Kader and others
full_judgment:
4. The trial court having decreed the suit and that having been affirmed by the lower appellate court by the impugned judgment and decree, and proceeding on the premise that both the courts below have decreed the suit on a misconception of law and gross misreading of materials on record, the Petitioner now contends that this has led to an error of law manifested in an erroneous decision occasioning a failure of justice. It is submitted specifically that inasmuch as according to the provisions of Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 earlier sale deeds take precedence over subsequent ones, the plaintiffs did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land on the basis of their subsequent alleged sale deeds of July 1978 (Exhibit- '1 series') as the sale property had already been sold to the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants by a registered sale deed dated 24.6.1960 (Exhibit-'M'). As executed, amongst others, by the alleged vendor of the plaintiffs, this relative status of the 1960 deed is submitted to be further enhanced by the very fact of it being a registered document that has a presumption of genuineness attached to it under Section 60 of the Registration Act, 1908, unless the contrary is proved which, it is submitted, has not been the case in this instance. In this regard, it has also been submitted in this Application that the suit is not maintainable without a concomitant prayer made for the cancellation of the sale deed of 24.6.1960 relied upon the defendants. It is also contended that both the courts below lost sight of the fact that the genealogy of the suit property given by the plaintiffs stood disproved given that P.S. Khatian No. 277 (Exhibit-'N') in respect of the non-disputed land clearly proved that Ramzan Ali had a son named Kala Miah who along with his two nephews executed the Exhibit 'M' sale deed of 24.6.1960 but which Kala Miah's existence is denied by the plaintiffs. It is submitted further that the impugned judgment not being in terms of Order 41, Rule 24 of the Code is not a proper judgment of affirmation in the eye of law inasmuch as the lower appellate court has endorsed the views of the trial court without any independent discussion and appreciation of materials on record. 

 7. It is on the above premise that this Court has had to consider the submissions of the learned Advocates of both parties as to the sufficiency or otherwise of the concurrent judgments of the courts below. The learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr. Mahmudul Islam has submitted that the registered kabala of 1960 is pivotal to an understanding of this case. Mr. Islam submits that the courts below erred in not finding that in light of there being a registered kabala of 1960 the vendor consequentially had no saleable interest in 1978. Rather, he submits, the courts below went in a roundabout manner in finding that the kabala of 1960 had not been acted upon. It is submitted that the Opposite Parties having in fact not made out a case in the plaint that the Petitioner's 1960 kabala was not acted upon, the trial court travelled well beyond the pleadings in that regard by finding on this issue. The learned Advocates for the Opposite Parties Dr. M. Zahir and Mr. Junayed Ahmed Chowdhury have submitted in response that the Opposite Parties had no direct or indirect knowledge of the existence of the 1960 sale deed prior to or during the institution of the suit even notwithstanding the fact that they otherwise remained diligent in examining the relevant records of rights and rent receipts that go to establish the title and possession of the vendor. It is pointed out in this regard, that it was the Petitioner himself who as defendant first introduced the fact of the existence of the 1960 sale deed in his written statement on the basis of which the trial court framed Issue No. 2 pertaining to determining the plaintiffs' title and interest in the suit land. That the trial court could so frame such an issue is clearly evident from the provisions of Order 14, Rule 3 of the Code that sanctions issues to be framed on the basis of all materials taken together as may be placed before the trial court in terms of pleadings and documentary evidence. As argued by the learned Advocates for the Opposite Parties the said Issue No. 2 so framed is sufficiently comprehensive as to bring within its ambit an examination and determination of the fact whether the 1960 sale deed had or had not been acted upon. This Court is satisfied that an enquiry in this regard was essential to determine the right and title of the Opposite Parties as would also necessarily entail adjudging on the validity of the 1978 sale deeds. It is in that context that the trial court undertook an examination of evidence as would establish the claim to possession of the suit land of one or the other of the parties. Taking the existence of the 1960 sale deed as a given, the trial court at the outset noted that not much evidence other than the registered kabala was forthcoming from the Petitioner in establishing the consequential exercise of possessory rights. In this regard, the trial court noted in particular both the failure of either the vendee Zakir Hossain and/or his sons to appear in court to prove the said sale deed as well as the absence of care evident in the failure to produce any other witness to prove the 1960 sale deed or to substantiate the fact of the vendee or his successors-in-interest ever having gone into possession of the suit land pursuant to such deed. That finding of the trial court is further fortified by its finding that the Petitioner at no point could establish the payment of rent on any material date for the material period given the failure in this regard to produce the relevant rent receipts before the court. On the other hand, the trial court aptly enquired into all documentary evidence produced by the Opposite Parties in evidence of the exercise of their possessory rights over the suit land as concomitantly established to the satisfaction of the court an unbroken chain of title and possession as stems from Fazlul Haque and continues down to the Opposite Parties. In this regard, the trial court took note of the record entries in the field survey khatian (Exhibit-'3K') as pertains to among others the Opposite Parties' predecessor-in-interest Fazlul Haque as well as Exhibit-'3 L' which is a mutation khatian favouring the Opposite Parties. In addition the trial court has found on the fact of the payments of rent for the suit land from the Exhibit- '4 series' rent receipts that show the Opposite Parties' predecessor-in-interest having continuously paid rent on the suit land from 1375 B.S. to 1382 B.S. that is, from approximately 1968 to 1975. It is evident further that the subsequent payments of rent have been made by the Opposite Parties themselves, a fact that is evident from the relevant rent receipts themselves as produced in evidence. In this Court's opinion, therefore, there is no reason why, and subscribing to the judgments in, for example, Akbar Ali and others v. Zahiruddin Kabri and others reported in 30 DLR (SC) 81 as well as Sultanuddsin Chowdhury v. Government of Bangladesh reported in 32 DLR (1980) 252 a presumption of possession from the above referred entries in the relevant records of rights may not arise given particularly where the correctness of such entries remain unimpeachable. Similarly unqualified would be the sanctity of such a presumption arising in the facts and circumstances from the fact of the production of the rent receipts as above noted (Erfan Ali v. Joynal Abedin reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216). 

 8. Pertinently, further, the trial court came to a finding that the presumption of possession as consequentially operates in favour of the Opposite Parties, though rebuttable, was not in fact rebutted by the Petitioner. It is also noted that this lapse on the part of the Petitioner had a bearing on the extent to which the fact of the dispossession of the Opposite Parties on 25.12.1978 could not be disproved to the satisfaction of the courts below. Indeed, as the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr. Mahmudul Islam has submitted before this Court, if the fact of such dispossession remains unsubstantiated the attendant presumption shall be of the Petitioner being in continuous possession since 1960. It has been asserted on behalf of the Petitioner in this regard that the Opposite Parties having produced no evidence of dispossession and thereby having not discharged their onus of proving the sale, the courts below erred by finding instead that the Petitioner had failed to discharge his burden in disproving the fact of dispossession. Though Mr. Mahmudul Islam has submitted that the Opposite Party No. 1 was evidently not a first-hand witness to the fact of dispossession as comes across in his statements given in cross-examination as P.W. 1, and the fact that the P.W. 2 did not depose at all on this issue, this issue has to be considered overall in the proper context of the fact, and as noted by the trial court itself, that the deposition and claim of the P.W.1 as to dispossession having remained unchallenged and uncontested on account of evidence to the contrary not being forthcoming from the Petitioner at all, the oral evidence given by the Opposite Parties as above remained acceptable as a given. It is noted that though the D.W.1 in his examination-in-chief denied the fact of dispossession, the vary fact of his acquaintance with the Petitioner dating back to only as recently as 1990, appropriately in the eyes of the courts below belied the veracity of his statements to that effect and made his credibility questionable. This Court therefore, finds itself in agreement with the trial court's finding on the issues of possession and dispossession as above. In this regard, this Court finds that given the fact that the Opposite Parties having discharged their burden of proof on the pleadings and that of adducing evidence with respect to possession and dispossession, that burden consequently shifted to the Petitioner not only to prove his continued possession from 1960 through to 25.12.1978, but concomitantly to disprove the dispossession of the Opposite Parties on 25.12.1978. This, and as is evident from the records made available to this Court, the Petitioner failed to do. These failings, in the view of this Court, thereby, cumulatively operated to establish in the minds of the courts below that the sale deed or kabala of 1960 was not duly acted upon by the Petitioner. That in these facts and circumstances the Petitioner's failure would inexorably lead to such unfavourable substantive consequences with the two courts below applying the judicially sanctified principles of discharge of burden of proof on the pleadings and the burden of proof on evidence, is well evident from the following enunciation in Kumbhan Lashmanna v. Tangirala Venkateshwarlu reported in 2 DLR 83 (PC): 

 9. Much has been said on behalf of the Petitioner in this Court on the issue of whether the courts below in their ostensible zeal for travelling beyond the pleadings made yet another case on the issue of adverse possession. Given that on a perusal of the judgments of the courts below it is evident to this Court that no finding on adverse possession was arrived at by the courts below as in any way detracts from or adds to the substantive findings on possession in particular and the merits of the case in general, this Court notes that it was indeed the learned Advocate of the defendant at the time taking a cue from the written statement itself who argued and submitted on the question of adverse possession that led the trial court, in addition to issues framed in the regular course, to also frame an additional issue on adverse possession, albeit by way of an observation. The actual and substantive findings of the trial court, and as endorsed by the lower appellate court as above quoted, in the view of this Court operate wholly and exclusively of the issue of adverse possession. In that regard, this Court finds itself to be in agreement with Dr. Zahir's argument that upon dwelling on these peripheral issues the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr. Mahmudul Islam has perhaps adopted a far too technical approach at deconstructing the judgments of the courts below. This Court therefore, finds itself to be equally in agreement with Dr. Zahir's submissions that the courts below did not err in identifying and deciding on the core issue of establishing and proving possession of the suit land. In this regard, this Court finds that both the courts below appropriately found for the Opposite Parties on the basis of uncontested oral and documentary evidence and presumptions that arise there from and which were not rebutted by the other party. That being the case this Court also finds that the lower appellate court at all times remained substantially in agreement with the trial court's judgment on these core issues and, therefore, there was no necessity for the said appellate court to proceed to further resettle any of the issues and, thereby, proceed to find otherwise than what had been arrived at by the trial court. By that reason this Court finds no justification as to how and why the provisions of Order 41, Rule 24 of the Code, as submitted on behalf of the Petitioner, can be said to be attracted to this case. 

 11. The provisions of Section 78 above clearly applying to instances where elements of gross neglect are found (Lloyds Bank Ltd. v. R E Guzdar Co. reported in AIR 1930 Calcutta, 22) and also having been found to apply to instances of sale (S. Arunachalam Asari and others v. Sivan Perumal Asari and another reported in AIR 1970 Madras, 226), it is not, therefore, difficult for this Court to subscribe to the ratio decidendi of the judgment in the Arunachalam Asari Case that the principle underlying Section 78 in applying to transactions of sale would accordingly operate to postpone the priority of a prior sale transaction should the prior vendee transferee be guilty of gross negligence. It is in that light that Mr. Junayed Ahmed Chowdhury has in particular submitted that the postponement of the rights created by the prior sale of 1960 shall operate in the facts and circumstances of this case given the Petitioner's gross negligence as evidenced in not acting upon the 1960 sale deed by taking the physical possession of the suit land at any material time or date, not being vigilant in amending the record of rights, thereby, allowing the name of the Opposite Parties' vendor to remain thereon and thereafter to be substituted by mutation in due process by the names of the Opposite Parties, and enabling at all material times the Opposite Parties' vendor and later the Opposite Parties, to pay rent for the suit land. These circumstances inexorably lead to the further conclusion that the Petitioner's indolence and/or negligence as above effectively allowed the vendor of the Opposite Parties to be in possession of the suit land for over twelve years i.e., eighteen years, till the execution of the above-referred deeds of 1978 favouring the Opposite Parties. This Court in this regard, finds merit in the submission so made and finds no reason why Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act shall be relied on in these circumstances to operate in favour of the Petitioner. It has also been argued on behalf of the Petitioner that by the time that the 1960 sale deed was produced before the trial court it qualified as a document to which certain presumptions attach pertaining to due registration under Section 60 of the Registration Act, 1908. On a perusal of the judgments of the courts below it is noted that there is no finding thereon that deny to the 1960 sale deed its status as a duly registered instrument. However, competing presumptions that have been found to operate in favour of the Opposite Parties' possessory rights, and duly so in the view of this Court, operate to discourage the attachment of any further significance to that act of registration of the 1960 sale deed as can otherwise create a dent in the relative strength of the presumptions duly found to be operating in favour of the Opposite Parties.
